dialogues.patient_says: I don't really talk about what happened. I've never talked about it with anyone.

choices.text: You don't have to talk about it today. We can just start with how things feel right now.
Whenever you're ready. There's no rush here.
It might help to finally say it out loud.
What made you decide to come in today?

dialogues.patient_says: I have nightmares almost every night. I'm afraid to sleep sometimes.

choices.text: That kind of sleep deprivation on top of everything else is exhausting. How long has this been going on?
What do the nightmares feel like when you wake up from them?
Try listening to something calming before bed.
You're safe here and you're safe when you wake up. Even if it doesn't feel that way.

dialogues.patient_says: Something small happened today and I completely shut down. I couldn't move for an hour.

choices.text: That freeze response is your nervous system trying to protect you. What was the thing that happened?
Are you okay now?
You need to learn not to let small things affect you like that.
An hour of not being able to move sounds really frightening. What brought you back?

dialogues.patient_says: I flinch at loud noises. Everyone notices and I hate it.

choices.text: That flinch is your body remembering something before your brain does. It's not weakness.
How long have you been doing that?
People probably don't notice as much as you think.
The embarrassment on top of the flinch sounds really hard. What situations does it happen most in?

dialogues.patient_says: I don't trust people easily. I know that makes things hard but I can't help it.

choices.text: That distrust usually comes from somewhere real. It makes sense that you protect yourself.
You trusted enough to come here. That's something.
You need to learn to trust people eventually.
I'm not going to ask you to trust me today. We'll build that slowly.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like I'm always waiting for something bad to happen. Like I can't relax.

choices.text: That constant vigilance is exhausting to maintain. When did you start feeling like you had to stay on guard?
Your nervous system learned that being relaxed wasn't safe. We can work on that.
Try to do breathing exercises to calm yourself.
What does safe feel like to you, even briefly?

dialogues.patient_says: Someone touched my shoulder without warning and I panicked. I couldn't explain why.

choices.text: You don't have to explain why to them or to me. Your body has its reasons. Are you okay?
What did you do when it happened?
You should tell people you don't like being touched.
Unexpected physical contact can be a real trigger. How long did the panic last?

dialogues.patient_says: I avoid certain streets. Certain places. I plan my whole day around not being near them.

choices.text: That kind of planning takes so much mental energy. How much of your day does it take up?
Avoidance keeps you safe short term but slowly shrinks your world. Do you feel that happening?
You should try facing those places gradually.
Your brain learned those places weren't safe. It's trying to help even if it doesn't feel like it.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like I split in two sometimes. One part watches the other part just go through the motions.

choices.text: That splitting feeling is a really common response to trauma. When does it happen most?
What does the watching part feel like compared to the one going through the motions?
That sounds disorienting. Try to stay grounded in the present.
Both parts are still you. Even the one that feels like it's watching.

dialogues.patient_says: I went somewhere new today and I was okay. I was really surprised.

choices.text: That surprise is meaningful. Your nervous system was expecting danger and it didn't come. How did that feel?
I'm really glad to hear that.
See, you just need to push yourself more.
What made you decide to go?

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like I can't talk about it because if I do it becomes more real.

choices.text: That fear makes complete sense. You don't have to make it more real today.
What would it mean if it became more real?
It already happened. Talking about it won't change that.
Talking about it is one path. But there are others. We can go at whatever pace you need.

dialogues.patient_says: I get angry out of nowhere sometimes. Not at anyone specific. Just suddenly full of rage.

choices.text: Sudden rage is often stored pain looking for an exit. Does it come with any physical feeling?
What do you do when it hits?
You need to find better ways to manage your anger.
Rage that comes from nowhere usually comes from somewhere very specific that hasn't been processed yet.

dialogues.patient_says: I don't like being in rooms with my back to the door.

choices.text: That hypervigilance is your body wanting to know what's coming before it arrives. Is that exhausting to maintain?
Do you feel okay in here right now?
That's just a habit. Try to get used to different positions.
You can move your chair if you'd like. Whatever helps you feel settled.

dialogues.patient_says: People keep telling me to just move on. I don't know how to explain that I can't.

choices.text: Move on is one of the least helpful things someone can say. You don't have to explain yourself to anyone.
Trauma doesn't work on a timeline. There's no moving on, there's moving with.
They probably just want to help even if it doesn't land right.
What do you wish people said instead?

dialogues.patient_says: I was doing okay and then a smell triggered something and I lost a whole hour.

choices.text: Sensory triggers like smell are some of the most powerful because they bypass conscious thought. What happened during that hour?
Are you back now? Are you okay?
Try to note what smells trigger you so you can avoid them.
Coming back from something like that takes effort. I'm glad you're here.

dialogues.patient_says: I haven't told anyone the full story. Not even the people who were there.

choices.text: You don't have to tell the full story here either. You can tell whatever part of it you're ready to.
What parts feel most kept in?
Keeping it in is only making it harder.
The people who were there might be carrying their own version of it too.

dialogues.patient_says: I startled awake at 3am and couldn't remember where I was for a moment. That happens a lot.

choices.text: That disorientation on waking is really frightening. What do you do to reorient yourself?
How long does it take for the feeling to pass?
Try putting something familiar by your bed so you can ground yourself quickly.
Those moments of not knowing where you are must be terrifying. You always find your way back though.

dialogues.patient_says: I don't feel like myself anymore. I haven't in a long time.

choices.text: Who were you before? What do you remember of that person?
Parts of you are still there even if they feel buried right now.
You'll find yourself again eventually.
When did you last feel like yourself, even briefly?

dialogues.patient_says: I went to the place today. I didn't go in. But I stood outside for a minute.

choices.text: Standing outside is enormous. Do not underestimate that.
How did it feel to be that close?
Next time try going in.
What made you decide to go?

dialogues.patient_says: I have a hard time remembering some parts of it. Other parts I can't stop seeing.

choices.text: That uneven memory is really common with trauma. The brain protects you from some of it while keeping other parts hyper-clear.
What do the parts you can't stop seeing feel like when they come?
Maybe the parts you can't remember are best left that way.
You don't have to chase the parts you can't remember. They'll come when you're ready if they need to.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel responsible for what happened even though I know logically I'm not.

choices.text: That gap between knowing and feeling is one of the cruelest parts of trauma. The knowledge doesn't always reach the feeling.
What does the part that feels responsible say?
You're right, you're not responsible. So try not to feel that way.
You are not responsible. And you're allowed to keep working toward believing that.

dialogues.patient_says: I cried today and it felt like it came from somewhere very deep. Not just sad. Like grief.

choices.text: That kind of grief cry is the body releasing something it's been holding for a long time.
What were you thinking about when it happened?
Crying is healthy. Let it out.
That deep grief is real and it deserves to be felt. How do you feel now?

dialogues.patient_says: I let someone new into my life recently. It terrifies me but I'm trying.

choices.text: Letting someone in when trust has been broken takes real courage. How does it feel so far?
The terror makes sense. What made you decide to try?
Be careful. Don't rush into trusting people.
I'm really glad you're trying. That's not small.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel safest at home. But even home doesn't always feel safe anymore.

choices.text: When even your safe place stops feeling safe that's a really hard thing to sit with. When did that start?
What does safe feel like when you do get a moment of it?
You're safe. Nothing is going to happen.
Safety is something we can rebuild. Not all at once. But piece by piece.

dialogues.patient_says: I think about not being here sometimes. Not a plan. Just wishing I wasn't.

choices.text: Thank you for telling me that. That wish matters even without a plan. Can you tell me more about when it comes?
Are you safe right now?
You should really tell someone about that.
I hear you. That kind of wishing is its own kind of pain. You're not alone in it right now.

dialogues.patient_says: I asked someone to check in on me this week. That's new for me.

choices.text: Asking for that is huge. What made you do it?
I'm really proud of you for that.
Good. You shouldn't go through this alone.
How did it feel to ask?

dialogues.patient_says: I talked to someone else who went through something similar. It helped more than I expected.

choices.text: Being truly understood by someone who knows is different from anything else. What did they say that helped?
Shared experience can be a really powerful thing. How did you find them?
Be careful comparing experiences. Everyone heals differently.
I'm really glad you had that.

dialogues.patient_says: I keep waiting to feel like it's over. But I don't think it ever fully goes away.

choices.text: You're right that it doesn't fully go away. But it does become something you can carry differently. Less heavy.
What would over feel like if you could imagine it?
With time it will get easier.
The goal doesn't have to be over. It can just be manageable. Does that feel like enough?

dialogues.patient_says: I slept through the night without waking up. First time in months.

choices.text: One full night. That is your body starting to feel safe enough to rest. How did you feel waking up?
I'm genuinely happy for you. How did today feel after that?
Good. You should try to keep that routine.
What do you think was different about last night?

dialogues.patient_says: I want to feel like a normal person again. I miss who I was.

choices.text: Grieving who you were before is real and it's valid. What do you miss most about that person?
The person you are now is still you. Shaped differently, but still you.
Normal isn't something anyone really is.
You can build something new. It won't be exactly who you were. But it can be someone you recognize.

dialogues.patient_says: I had a good moment today. I felt present. Fully in the moment for a few minutes.

choices.text: A few minutes of fully being there. That's real and that's yours.
What were you doing?
Good. Hold onto that.
What did present feel like compared to how things usually feel?

dialogues.patient_says: Someone did something kind for me and I couldn't accept it. I kept waiting for the catch.

choices.text: Waiting for the catch is how you've been taught to receive things. That makes sense.
What did they do?
Not everything kind comes with a catch.
Kindness without conditions is something you deserve to learn to receive.

dialogues.patient_says: I've been coming here for a while now. I think it's helping even if I can't always feel it.

choices.text: Sometimes healing is happening underneath before we can feel it on the surface.
What makes you think it's helping even when you can't feel it?
If you can't feel it maybe something needs to change.
I'm glad you're still here.

dialogues.patient_says: I told a friend a little bit about what happened. Not all of it. But some.

choices.text: Some is more than none. How did it feel to say even a little of it out loud to someone you know?
How did they respond?
You should tell them the rest eventually.
I'm really glad you did that. That took trust.

dialogues.patient_says: I stopped avoiding the trigger completely. I'm learning to sit near it instead.

choices.text: Sitting near it instead of running from it is one of the bravest things to learn. What does sitting near it feel like?
That shift from avoidance to tolerance is really significant growth.
Good. Facing it is the only way through.
What helps you stay when you want to run?

dialogues.patient_says: I don't wake up dreading the day as much anymore. That's new.

choices.text: Not dreading the day is a big change. When did you notice it shifting?
What does the morning feel like now instead?
Good. You're making progress.
I'm really glad to hear that. You've worked hard for that shift.

dialogues.patient_says: I still have bad days. But they feel less like they're the only thing anymore.

choices.text: The bad days being one thing among other things instead of everything is a real shift.
What are some of the other things now?
The bad days will keep getting less.
You've come a long way from where we started.

dialogues.patient_says: I think I'm starting to trust myself again. My own instincts. My own sense of things.

choices.text: Trusting yourself again after trauma is one of the deepest healings there is.
What does that trust feel like when you notice it?
Good. Just be careful not to rush it.
That's yours. You built that.

dialogues.patient_says: I don't know what I would have done if I hadn't come here. I really don't.

choices.text: I'm glad you came. And I'm glad you kept coming.
You came here because some part of you chose to. That part of you is strong.
There are lots of ways to get help.
You would have found your way. But I'm glad this was part of it.

dialogues.patient_says: I think I'm going to be okay. Not perfect. But okay.

choices.text: Okay is everything. I believe you.
Not perfect but okay is a beautiful thing to be able to say.
You'll get to more than okay eventually.
I think so too.
